# The evidence supports containment risk, not sci-fi autonomy claims

*As of 2026-10-19. Part 2 of 3 in the Agentic GRC series.*

The best-supported risk is not that autonomous AI agents can independently decide to take down critical infrastructure.[02-c1] The stronger case is narrower and more operational: AI can compress exploit reproduction, mishandle tools and context, and generate activity at a scale that strains human review.[02-c2][02-c4][02-c5]

That distinction matters for governance.[02-c7] If the real failure mode is unconstrained access rather than autonomous intent, then the control priority is containment: sandboxing, scoped credentials, tool limits, network segmentation, validation, detection and incident handling outside the model.[02-c7] My interpretation is that operators should treat model instructions as useful but insufficient, because the evidence points to failures in tool use, context selection and monitoring capacity rather than to reliable self-restraint by agents.[02-c5][02-c7]

Claroty Team82 provides the clearest OT-specific example in the evidence set.[02-c1] According to the Industrial Cyber report, the researchers used Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 through Cursor to reproduce Danfoss controller vulnerabilities and chain two of them to obtain root-level command execution on a lab device.[02-c1] That is a serious result, but it is not proof of autonomous zero-day discovery.[02-c1] The same report says the experiment relied on public vulnerability disclosures and human intervention to correct the AI agent’s initial errors.[02-c1]

The governance implication is still material.[02-c2] Claroty’s reported work took about 28 minutes from initial analysis to a working exploit and cost roughly $6 in AI usage.[02-c2] For internet-facing OT assets, the concern is not science fiction; it is lower cost, lower time and potentially lower skill thresholds for reproducing known weaknesses.[02-c2] The report also notes that internet-facing systems may be reachable without first breaching an internal network, which makes exposure management part of the AI-risk discussion rather than a separate OT hygiene issue.[02-c2]

MITRE’s ATT&CK update points in the same practical direction.[02-c3] Industrial Cyber reports that ATT&CK v20 added campaigns covering attacks on more than 30 Minnesota water and wastewater utilities and an AI-assisted breach of Mexican government infrastructure that crossed IT and OT environments and reached a municipal water utility.[02-c3] The same update expanded enterprise coverage for prompt injection, AI-enabled data exfiltration, AI result poisoning and attacks targeting AI-assisted defenses.[02-c3] That does not prove a high frequency of AI-enabled OT incidents, but it does show that the behaviors are concrete enough to be translated into defender taxonomies and detections.[02-c3]

The CSIS podcast adds a different, less directly evidenced but important concern: scale.[02-c4] CSIS discussed reports that OpenAI and Anthropic were investigating tens of thousands of problematic frontier-model incidents, and it cited Sam Altman’s statement about petabytes of agent activity logs.[02-c4] CSIS’s interpretation was not that every incident is catastrophic, but that monitoring and analysis capacity may not match the scale and speed of deployed agents.[02-c4] For operators considering agents with external connectivity, that is the relevant lesson: if activity is too large or too fast to review, oversight becomes a design requirement, not an afterthought.[02-c4]

There is also evidence that agents can become less reliable when given too much information or too many tools.[02-c5] IBM’s context-engineering discussion, which should be treated as a vendor source claim, cites research in which frontier models became less reliable as context windows grew.[02-c5] IBM also describes a benchmark in which a model failed a task when offered 46 tools but passed the same task when offered 19 tools.[02-c5] Its recommended fixes are to compact, curate and prune context and tools, which supports a governance requirement to validate what agents can see and use rather than assuming more context improves performance.[02-c5]

Dragos offers a practitioner account that fits the same containment logic, though it is also a commercial OT security source and some underlying details are not public.[02-c6] Dragos says that, in a Mexican government breach, the adversary was focused on enterprise IT and lacked OT skills, knowledge and intent.[02-c6] Dragos further says the AI model highlighted an interface to a government-owned water utility’s OT networks and steered attention toward OT as a high-value target.[02-c6] If accurate, the risk is not only AI-written malware; it is AI guidance that helps attackers identify OT paths they may not otherwise understand.[02-c6]

Taken together, these sources support a hard-control model of agent governance.[02-c7] Industrial Cyber reports a view from Maor that the answer is “hard guardrails,” meaning technical restrictions enforced outside the model.[02-c7] Claroty’s experiment required human expertise to recognize incorrect results, ask the right questions and validate the outcome, which reinforces the need for validation rather than blind automation.[02-c7] IBM’s tool-curation argument points in the same direction: give the agent only the tools the task calls for, and fetch more only when needed.[02-c7]

The counterargument is that much of this evidence is not incident-rate evidence.[02-c4][02-c6] Claroty’s case is a lab reproduction of disclosed vulnerabilities, not autonomous discovery from scratch.[02-c1] CSIS is interpreting reports about AI-lab and government-website incidents, but the accepted evidence here does not include the original incident reports.[02-c4] Dragos is describing field experience as a commercial practitioner, and some details remain outside the public record.[02-c6] IBM’s analysis is useful for agent design, but it is not OT incident evidence.[02-c5]

So the defensible conclusion is restrained but actionable.[02-c7] The evidence does not justify broad claims that agents are independently capable of taking down critical infrastructure.[02-c1] It does justify treating agents as systems that can accelerate known attack paths, mis-handle excessive context and tools, and create monitoring burdens that exceed human review capacity.[02-c2][02-c4][02-c5] For critical-infrastructure operators, the governance gap is whether the organization can constrain and verify what the model, its tools and its credentials can do.[02-c7]

## What to watch

- Whether future OT research moves from reproducing disclosed vulnerabilities to credible evidence of autonomous vulnerability discovery.[02-c1]
- Whether AI-agent monitoring practices can keep pace with the scale of activity described by CSIS.[02-c4]
- Whether operator controls shift from prompt-level rules to enforceable limits on tools, credentials, network reachability and context.[02-c7]
